2004-Q12a.q: What is the kidneys' main job in homeostasis?
2004-Q12a.right: Balancing the body's water and salt levels
wrong: Making urea from excess amino acids
2004-Q12a.why: The kidneys keep water and salt levels steady (osmoregulation); urea is made in the liver, not the kidneys.

2004-Q12b.q: On a nephron diagram, which vessel carries blood into the glomerulus?
2004-Q12b.why: The afferent arteriole brings blood in (a for arrive); the efferent arteriole takes it out (e for exit).

2004-Q12b.q: Which best describes filtration in the nephron?
2004-Q12b.right: Pressure forces plasma into Bowman's capsule
wrong: Active transport pumps cells into the capsule
Osmosis draws proteins into Bowman's capsule
Pressure forces plasma into the loop of Henle
2004-Q12b.why: Blood in the glomerulus is under high pressure, so plasma and small molecules are squeezed into Bowman's capsule.

2005-Q1f.q: Getting rid of the waste made by metabolism is called what?
2005-Q1f.why: Excretion removes waste cells make, like urea and CO2; egestion removes undigested food that cells never made.

2005-Q3a.q: True or false: urea is made in the kidneys.
2005-Q3a.why: Urea is made in the liver by deamination; the kidneys only filter it out of the blood.

2006-Q6b.q: Which tube carries urine from the kidney to the bladder?
2006-Q6b.why: The ureter runs from kidney to bladder; the urethra carries urine from the bladder out of the body.

2006-Q13b.right: Plasma without proteins, in Bowman's capsule
wrong: Plasma with its proteins, in Bowman's capsule
Blood cells left behind in the glomerulus
Concentrated urine in the collecting duct
2006-Q13b.why: Filtrate is plasma squeezed into Bowman's capsule; proteins and blood cells are too big to get through.

2006-Q13b.q: Why are red blood cells missing from glomerular filtrate?
2006-Q13b.right: They are too big to pass into the capsule
wrong: They are reabsorbed in the proximal tubule
They are broken down in the glomerulus
ADH stops them leaving the blood vessels
2006-Q13b.why: Red cells are far too big to squeeze through the glomerulus wall into Bowman's capsule, so they stay in the blood.

2006-Q13b.q: Why does filtrate have the same glucose level as plasma?
2006-Q13b.right: Glucose is small and passes freely through
wrong: Glucose is pumped in by active transport
Insulin pushes glucose into the capsule
Glucose is made by cells of the capsule
2006-Q13b.why: Glucose molecules are small enough to be filtered freely, so filtrate gets the same glucose level as plasma.

2006-Q13b.q: Why is there normally no glucose in urine?
2006-Q13b.right: It is all reabsorbed into the blood
wrong: It is too big to pass into the capsule
It is turned into urea in the kidney
ADH stops it from being filtered
2006-Q13b.why: Glucose is filtered, but the proximal tubule reabsorbs all of it back into the blood, so none reaches the urine.

2006-Q13b.q: After heavy exercise, why is a small volume of concentrated urine made?
2006-Q13b.right: More ADH, so more water is reabsorbed
wrong: More ADH, so less water is reabsorbed
Less ADH, so less water is reabsorbed
More insulin, so more water is reabsorbed
2006-Q13b.why: Sweating dehydrates you, so the pituitary releases more ADH and the tubules reabsorb more water into the blood.

2007-Q15c.q: Why is homeostasis important in the body?
2007-Q15c.right: Keeps conditions right for enzymes to work
wrong: Lets body temperature follow the surroundings
Stops the body needing to excrete wastes
Removes undigested food from the body
2007-Q15c.why: A steady internal environment keeps temperature and pH right, so enzymes and metabolism work properly.

2008-Q13a.right: Removing waste made by the body's metabolism
wrong: Removing undigested food from the gut
Releasing useful substances such as hormones
2008-Q13a.why: Excretion gets rid of waste made by cells, like urea and CO2; removing undigested food is egestion.

2008-Q13a.q: Urea is made from which substance?
2008-Q13a.why: Excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver and their nitrogen becomes urea; fats and sugars contain no nitrogen.

2008-Q13b.q: On the diagram, which part is C?
2008-Q13b.why: C comes straight after Bowman's capsule, so it is the proximal (first) tubule; the distal one comes after the loop.

2008-Q13b.q: Arteriole A branches from which blood vessel?
2008-Q13b.why: The renal artery brings blood into the kidney and branches into the arterioles that feed each glomerulus.

2008-Q13b.q: In which region of the kidney is Bowman's capsule (B)?
2008-Q13b.why: Bowman's capsules and glomeruli sit in the outer cortex; the loops of Henle dip down into the medulla.

2008-Q13b.q: In which part of the nephron are amino acids reabsorbed?
2008-Q13b.why: The proximal tubule reabsorbs all the glucose and amino acids; later parts mainly handle water and salts.

2008-Q13b.q: Which feature of the nephron helps filtration?
wrong: Few, wide capillaries in the glomerulus
2008-Q13b.why: A narrow exit vessel backs blood up in the glomerulus, raising the pressure that forces filtrate out.

2008-Q13b.q: Which group of biomolecules is too big to be filtered?
2008-Q13b.why: Proteins are big molecules that can't pass through the glomerulus wall; glucose and amino acids are small.

2008-Q13c.q: Which could lower the water content of the blood?
wrong: Eating very little salt in food
2008-Q13c.why: Sweat takes water out of the body, so the blood loses water; drinking and ADH both help keep water in.

2008-Q13c.q: Which gland secretes ADH when blood water drops?
2008-Q13c.why: ADH is released by the pituitary gland at the base of the brain; the adrenal glands on the kidneys make adrenaline.

2008-Q13c.q: Where in the nephron does ADH act?
2008-Q13c.why: ADH travels in the blood to the collecting duct (and distal tubule) and makes their walls let water back out.

2008-Q13c.q: When blood water is low, what does ADH do at its target?
2008-Q13c.right: More water is reabsorbed into the blood
wrong: More water is released into the urine
More glucose is reabsorbed into the blood
Less water is reabsorbed into the blood
2008-Q13c.why: ADH makes the duct walls more permeable to water, so more water moves back into the blood and less is lost.

2009-Q15c.q: Which is an example of homeostasis?
2009-Q15c.right: Sweating to cool down when hot
wrong: Shivering to cool down when hot
2009-Q15c.why: Sweat evaporates and carries heat away, keeping body temperature steady; shivering warms you up.

2010-Q15c.q: Which chain explains the athlete's concentrated urine?
2010-Q15c.right: Sweat loss, more ADH, more water reabsorbed
wrong: Sweat loss, less ADH, more water reabsorbed
Sweat loss, more ADH, less water reabsorbed
Extra urea, less ADH, less water reabsorbed
2010-Q15c.why: Losing water in sweat leaves less water in the blood, so more ADH is released and the ducts reabsorb more water.

2011-Q12a.right: Getting rid of waste made by body cells
wrong: Getting rid of food that was never digested
Releasing enzymes and hormones from glands
Breaking food down into small molecules
2011-Q12a.why: Excretion removes wastes your own cells make, like urea; getting rid of undigested food is egestion.

2011-Q12b.q: On a kidney section, which region collects urine before the ureter?
2011-Q12b.why: The pelvis is the hollow space in the middle where urine collects before draining into the ureter.

2011-Q12b.q: On a kidney section, where does reabsorption happen?
2011-Q12b.right: In the tubules of the cortex and medulla
wrong: In the pelvis, where urine collects
In the ureter, leaving the kidney
In the renal vein, leaving the kidney
2011-Q12b.why: Reabsorption happens in the nephron tubules, found in the cortex and medulla; the pelvis and ureter only carry urine.

2011-Q12b.q: The renal artery branches off which blood vessel?
2011-Q12b.why: The renal arteries branch straight off the aorta, the main artery from the heart; the vena cava is a vein.

2011-Q12b.q: In which body cavity are the kidneys?
2011-Q12b.why: The kidneys sit at the back of the abdomen, below the diaphragm; the thoracic cavity holds the heart and lungs.

2011-Q12b.q: Which substance, other than water, is excreted in urine?
2011-Q12b.why: Urea, made from excess amino acids in the liver, leaves in urine; glucose and amino acids are normally reabsorbed.

2011-Q12b.q: What shows the kidney works like an exocrine gland?
2011-Q12b.right: It releases its product through a duct
wrong: It releases hormones into the blood
It has a very rich blood supply
It filters blood under high pressure
2011-Q12b.why: Exocrine glands release their products through ducts; urine leaves the kidney through a duct, the ureter.

2011-Q12c.q: On the diagram, what is part 4?
2011-Q12c.why: Part 4 carries blood out of the glomerulus: the efferent arteriole (e for exit); the afferent one brings blood in.

2011-Q12c.q: Is protein in urine normal, and why?
2011-Q12c.right: No, proteins are too big to be filtered
wrong: Yes, proteins are small enough to filter
Yes, proteins are a normal waste product
No, ADH stops proteins being filtered
2011-Q12c.why: Protein molecules are too big to pass through the glomerulus wall, so protein in urine suggests kidney damage.

2011-Q12c.q: Is glucose in urine normal, and why?
2011-Q12c.right: No, all glucose should be reabsorbed
wrong: No, glucose is too big to be filtered
Yes, extra glucose is a waste product
2011-Q12c.why: Glucose is filtered, but the proximal tubule should reabsorb all of it; glucose in urine can be a sign of diabetes.

wrong: Removing the waste products of metabolism
2012-Q15c.why: Homeostasis keeps conditions inside the body, like temperature, pH and water, steady; removing waste is excretion.

2012-Q15c.q: How does the liver help homeostasis?
2012-Q15c.right: Stores or releases glucose as needed
wrong: Filters urea out of the blood into urine
Excretes carbon dioxide from the body
Secretes insulin to lower blood sugar
2012-Q15c.why: The liver stores glucose as glycogen and releases it when needed; insulin comes from the pancreas, not the liver.

2016-Q12a.right: Removing undigested material from the gut
wrong: Removing waste made by cell metabolism
Removing urea from the blood in urine
Releasing digestive enzymes into the gut
2016-Q12a.why: Egestion gets rid of food that was never absorbed into cells; excretion removes waste that cells have made.

2016-Q12b.q: Which is an excretory product of mammals, other than water?
2016-Q12b.why: CO2 is a waste made by respiration in cells, so removing it is excretion; fibre is undigested food (egestion).

2016-Q12b.q: Where in the body is carbon dioxide produced?
2016-Q12b.right: In all body cells, by respiration
wrong: Only in the lungs, by breathing
2016-Q12b.why: Every cell makes CO2 in respiration; the lungs only remove it from the body. (Urea is the one made in the liver.)

2016-Q12b.q: Which best describes what ADH does?
2016-Q12b.right: Ducts reabsorb more water, so less urine forms
wrong: Ducts reabsorb less water, so more urine forms
Ducts reabsorb more salt, so more urine forms
Glomerulus filters more, so more urine forms
2016-Q12b.why: ADH makes collecting duct walls more permeable, so more water goes back to the blood and urine is concentrated.

2016-Q12c.q: What does the term homeostasis mean?
wrong: Removing undigested food from the body
2016-Q12c.why: Homeostasis keeps the inside of the body steady (temperature, pH, water) even when the outside changes.

2016-Q15a.q: Which vein carries blood away from the kidneys?
2016-Q15a.why: The renal vein drains blood from each kidney to the vena cava; the renal artery brings blood in.

2017-Q14c.q: Which feature helps the glomerulus filter blood?
2017-Q14c.right: Capillary walls only one cell thick
wrong: Thick muscular walls to resist pressure
Low blood pressure in its capillaries
A small surface area to limit loss
2017-Q14c.why: Thin capillary walls let small molecules pass out easily; high pressure and a large surface area also help.

2017-Q15a.right: Keeping conditions inside the body steady
wrong: Keeping conditions outside the body steady
Getting rid of waste made by cells
Breaking food down to release energy
2017-Q15a.why: Homeostasis is about the internal environment staying constant; getting rid of cell waste is excretion.

2017-Q15a.q: Why does the body need homeostasis?
2017-Q15a.right: So enzymes get the right temperature and pH
wrong: So the body no longer needs to excrete
So blood glucose can rise freely after meals
So body temperature can match the weather
2017-Q15a.why: Enzymes only work well in a narrow range of temperature and pH, so keeping these steady keeps metabolism going.

2018-Q6.q: On the diagram, which structure is Y?
2018-Q6.why: Y comes after the loop of Henle, so it is the distal (far) tubule; the proximal one is right after Bowman's capsule.

2018-Q6.q: Where on the diagram does ADH act?
2018-Q6.why: ADH targets the collecting duct (and distal tubule), the last parts of the nephron, where water can be saved.

2018-Q6.q: What does ADH do to its target area?
2018-Q6.right: Makes it more permeable to water
wrong: Makes it less permeable to water
Makes it pump glucose into urine
Makes it let protein into urine
2018-Q6.why: With ADH the duct walls let more water through, so more water is reabsorbed into the blood.

2018-Q6.q: What change in the blood triggers ADH release?
2018-Q6.right: Higher salt, less water in the blood
wrong: Lower salt, more water in the blood
Higher carbon dioxide in the blood
2018-Q6.why: When blood gets too salty (too little water), the brain detects it and ADH is released to save water.

2018-Q6.q: In which gland is ADH made?
2018-Q6.why: ADH is made in the hypothalamus and released from the pituitary; the scheme accepts either.

2018-Q6.q: Which is a treatment for kidney failure?
2018-Q6.why: A dialysis machine filters urea and extra salt from the blood when the kidneys fail; a transplant also works.

wrong: Changing body temperature with the weather
2020-Q13a.why: Homeostasis keeps the body's internal conditions steady; removing metabolic waste is excretion.

2020-Q13a.q: Why is homeostasis important in organisms?
2020-Q13a.right: Lets enzymes and metabolism work properly
wrong: Stops cells from needing any energy
Lets body pH change freely with diet
Lets cells take in water without limit
2020-Q13a.why: Enzymes need a steady temperature and pH, so a constant internal environment keeps metabolism running well.

2020-Q13a.right: Removal of metabolic waste from the body
wrong: Removal of undigested food from the body
Release of energy from food in cells
2020-Q13a.why: Excretion removes waste made by metabolism, like urea and CO2; removing undigested food is egestion.

2020-Q13b.q: Where in the body is urea made?
2020-Q13b.why: The liver breaks down excess amino acids (deamination) to make urea; the kidneys only remove it.

2020-Q13b.q: Which food biomolecule is urea made from?
2020-Q13b.why: Proteins contain nitrogen; extra amino acids are deaminated and the nitrogen ends up in urea. Carbs and fats have none.

2020-Q13b.q: In which part of the kidney is the loop of Henle found?
2020-Q13b.why: The loops of Henle dip down into the medulla; Bowman's capsules and the convoluted tubules are in the cortex.

2020-Q13b.q: In order, which parts follow Bowman's capsule in a nephron?
2020-Q13b.right: PCT, loop of Henle, DCT, collecting duct
wrong: DCT, loop of Henle, PCT, collecting duct
Loop of Henle, PCT, DCT, collecting duct
PCT, DCT, loop of Henle, collecting duct
2020-Q13b.why: Filtrate flows from the capsule to the proximal tubule (PCT), down the loop of Henle, to the distal tubule (DCT).

2020-Q13c.q: From the table, how does plasma differ from filtrate?
2020-Q13c.right: Plasma has proteins; filtrate has none
wrong: Plasma has glucose; filtrate has none
Filtrate has proteins; plasma has none
Plasma has more urea than filtrate
2020-Q13c.why: Plasma has 7 g of protein per 100 cm3 and filtrate has none, as proteins are too big to pass into the capsule.

2020-Q13c.q: From the table, why is there glucose in filtrate but none in urine?
2020-Q13c.right: All the glucose is reabsorbed into blood
wrong: Glucose is too big to enter the filtrate
Glucose is turned into urea in the tubule
Glucose is used up by the bladder wall
2020-Q13c.why: Glucose is filtered (0.1 in both plasma and filtrate), then all of it is reabsorbed in the tubule, so urine has 0.

2020-Q13c.q: What does a high salt intake do to urine volume, and why?
2020-Q13c.right: Less urine, as more ADH is released
wrong: More urine, as more ADH is released
More urine, as less ADH is released
Less urine, as less ADH is released
2020-Q13c.why: Salty blood triggers more ADH, so the collecting ducts reabsorb more water and less urine is made.

wrong: Removing toxic waste made by cells
2021-Q15a.why: Homeostasis means the body keeps its inside conditions, like temperature and water level, stable.

2022-Q15a.q: Which of these is the meaning of excretion?
2022-Q15a.right: Removing metabolic waste from a cell
wrong: Removing undigested food from the gut
2022-Q15a.why: Excretion removes waste made by metabolism; keeping a constant internal environment is homeostasis.

2022-Q15b.q: What does the fat layer around the kidneys do?
2022-Q15b.right: Protects them from knocks and bumps
wrong: Stores urine before it goes to the bladder
Makes ADH to control water balance
2022-Q15b.why: The fat cushions the kidneys against knocks (and insulates them); urine is stored in the bladder, not the fat.

2022-Q15b.q: On the kidney diagram, which region is B?
2022-Q15b.why: B is the middle layer with the pyramids: the medulla. The cortex (A) is outside it and the pelvis (C) inside.

2022-Q15b.q: In which kidney region does filtration happen?
2022-Q15b.why: Filtration happens at the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule, which are found in the outer cortex.

2022-Q15b.q: Why does blood enter the glomerulus under high pressure?
2022-Q15b.right: To force small molecules out into the capsule
wrong: To force proteins out into the capsule
To push filtrate back into the blood
To stop any plasma leaving the blood
2022-Q15b.why: High pressure squeezes water and small molecules out of the blood into Bowman's capsule: that is filtration.

2022-Q15b.q: Why are the tubules wrapped in so many capillaries?
wrong: To make ADH for the tubule walls
To carry urine down to the bladder
To push proteins into the filtrate
2022-Q15b.why: Water, glucose and salts reabsorbed from the tubules pass straight into these capillaries and go back to the blood.

2022-Q15b.q: How does more ADH change urine volume?
2022-Q15b.right: Lowers it: more water is reabsorbed
wrong: Raises it: less water is reabsorbed
Lowers it: less water is filtered
Raises it: more salt is excreted
2022-Q15b.why: ADH makes the collecting duct more permeable, so more water returns to the blood and a small volume of urine forms.

2022-Q15b.q: Urine leaves C and travels to the bladder through which tube?
2022-Q15b.why: The ureter carries urine from the kidney's pelvis to the bladder; the urethra takes it from the bladder out.

2023-Q6d.q: Why is urine volume low if you don't drink much?
2023-Q6d.why: Low water in the blood triggers more ADH, so the collecting ducts reabsorb more water and less urine is made.

2023-Q17c.q: Which vein carries blood with the least metabolic waste?
2023-Q17c.why: Blood leaving the kidneys has just had urea and other wastes filtered out, so the renal vein has the least.

2024-Q17c.q: What is the name for keeping a constant internal environment?
2024-Q17c.why: Homeostasis is the general term; osmoregulation is just the water and salt part of it.

2024-Q17c.q: On a nephron diagram, which structure cups the glomerulus?
2024-Q17c.why: Bowman's capsule is the cup that wraps around the glomerulus and collects the filtrate.

2024-Q17c.q: Which is a way blood differs from glomerular filtrate?
2024-Q17c.right: Blood has cells; filtrate has none
wrong: Filtrate has cells; blood has none
Blood has glucose; filtrate has none
Blood has urea; filtrate has none
2024-Q17c.why: Blood cells (and plasma proteins) are too big to be filtered; glucose and urea pass into the filtrate.

2024-Q17c.q: Which part of the nephron reabsorbs water?
2024-Q17c.why: Water is reabsorbed along the tubules (PCT, loop, DCT, collecting duct); the glomerulus is where filtering happens.

wrong: Maintaining a constant rate of growth
Removing metabolic waste from the body
2025-Q17c.why: Homeostasis keeps internal conditions like temperature, pH and water constant; removing waste is excretion.
ADH is released from the pituitary at the base of the brain; the adrenal glands make adrenaline.

2025-Q17c.q: Which part of the nephron does ADH affect?
2025-Q17c.why: ADH acts on the distal tubule and collecting duct, making their walls let more water back into the blood.

2025-Q17c.q: What does more ADH do to the volume of urine?
2025-Q17c.why: More ADH means more water is reabsorbed, so a smaller volume of more concentrated urine is made.

2025-Q17c.q: From the graphs, how do blood volume and ADH change during exercise?
2025-Q17c.right: Blood volume falls as ADH rises
wrong: Blood volume rises as ADH rises
Blood volume falls as ADH falls
Blood volume falls, ADH stays level
2025-Q17c.why: Sweating cuts blood volume, so more ADH is released to save water: volume goes down while ADH goes up.

2025-Q17c.q: Which is a way the skin helps the athlete's homeostasis?
wrong: Shivering, so muscles make extra heat
Absorbing water to replace what's lost
Releasing ADH to reduce water loss
2025-Q17c.why: Sweat on the skin evaporates and carries heat away; shivering is done by muscles and warms you up.

2026-Q17b.q: What is the ability to keep a constant internal environment called?
2026-Q17b.why: Homeostasis covers all internal conditions; thermoregulation only covers temperature.

2026-Q17b.q: Why must organisms keep a constant internal environment?
wrong: So body temperature can match the air
So no waste is ever produced
So cells can take in water freely
2026-Q17b.why: Enzymes need the right temperature and pH; keeping these constant lets metabolism run efficiently.

2026-Q17c.right: Removing the waste products of metabolism
wrong: Taking useful substances back into blood
2026-Q17c.why: Excretion removes waste made by the body's chemical reactions, like urea; removing fibre is egestion.

2026-Q17c.q: Which way should the urine arrow on the ureter point?
2026-Q17c.why: Urine is made in the kidney and flows down the ureter into the bladder; the urethra then carries it out.

2026-Q17c.q: In part B (loop of Henle), what happens?
wrong: ADH is made and sent to the blood
Glucose is moved into the urine
2026-Q17c.why: The loop of Henle reabsorbs water and salts; filtering under pressure happens at A, Bowman's capsule.

2026-Q17c.q: Why is there normally no protein in urine?
2026-Q17c.right: Protein is too big to be filtered
wrong: Protein is turned into urea first
Protein is used up by kidney cells
2026-Q17c.why: Protein molecules are too big to pass through the glomerulus wall into Bowman's capsule, so they stay in the blood.

S1-Q1e.q: On the diagram, which part is A?
S1-Q1e.why: A comes straight after Bowman's capsule, before the loop of Henle, so it is the proximal (first) tubule.

S1-Q1e.q: Where on the diagram should you write F for ultrafiltration?
S1-Q1e.why: Ultrafiltration happens where blood under pressure in the glomerulus is squeezed into Bowman's capsule.

S1-Q1e.q: Which part of the blood is not normally found in urine?
S1-Q1e.why: Plasma proteins are too big to be filtered; urea, water and salts all end up in urine.

S1-Q1e.q: How does a longer loop of Henle help a desert animal?
S1-Q1e.right: More water is reabsorbed into the blood
wrong: More water is lost in dilute urine
Blood is filtered at a higher pressure
More glucose is reabsorbed into the blood
S1-Q1e.why: A longer loop lets more water be reabsorbed, so the animal makes concentrated urine and saves water.
